newsitem.title: ITALY: No frills at low-cost World Food Summit in Rome.
newsitem.headline: No frills at low-cost World Food Summit in Rome.

text.p: Benito Mussolini would have been proud.

Many of the world's leaders will gather in Rome this week in a building the Fascist Duce ordered built in 1935 to house his "Ministry for an Italian Africa" as part of his brutal and disastrous dream of colonial rule.
Bombastic, labyrinthine and a discoloured a dirty white by the traffic exhaust smog that envelops Rome, it has been home since 1951 to the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation.
From Wednesday, it will be very crowded place as several thousand delegates and journalists descend on the Italian capital for FAO's five-day World Food Summit.

Aware of criticism that past U.N. conferences have devoured cash better spent on the problems they were called to tackle, FAO director general Jacques Diouf of Senegal insisted that this week's event should be a low-cost, no-frills affair.
Delegations have been told not to splash out on lavish receptions lest they be deemed to be spending more time eating than discussing responses to hunger in the world.
The agency, with 174 member states, had just $1.27 million to spend on the summit and $840,000 more on staff. Thus the decision to meet at the headquarters rather than go elsewhere.
To make room for the visitors, staff have had to vacate their offices. Orders to go on leave or work from home have raised more than a few grumbles among the multinational ranks.
The FAO mail despatch room has found a new lease of life as the main news conference room.
Diouf, 58, who was elected to FAO's top job in 1993, believes staff will ultimately benefit from the inconvenience.

"We...innovated by making sure that the summit is held in our building," Douf told Reuters on Tuesday. "That allowed us to improve our building, to improve our environment for work and naturally to cut our costs because nobody travels."
But many Romans were wondering on Tuesday how they would travel during the summit, with around 10,000 police on duty to guard the high-level delegations.

Roads around the building, a brief chariot ride from the ancient Colosseum, are among the main arteries to the city centre. They will be closed throughout the event along with the nearest metro station.
"It's like this now," said one taxi driver gloomily surveying the traffic jam on the road leading to FAO headquarters. "Just wait until it rains."
